$comment: Run, bike and swim. Separate from program.json because it is not organised by gym day and does
not have a set/rep/rest shape. Evidence for every number is in
HealthOS/knowledge/training-programme-evidence.md.
THE SCHEDULING RULE THAT MAKES THIS FIT, and the reason nothing he already does had to be
traded away: Robineau 2016 found strength gains were LOWER when the aerobic piece followed the
lift immediately (0 h) than at 6 h or 24 h. So the running goes in a morning slot he is not
currently using, against a 9 pm swim that is 12+ hours away.
His lift-then-swim stack on the same evening is inside that 6 h window and STAYS ANYWAY. He has
done it for months and the back squat went 135 to 180 lb across that period. His own log
outranks a guideline derived from rugby players doing a different pairing.
TECHNIQUE CUES, added 2026-08-16. He had never run or cycled and the plan told him how HARD and
how LONG and never HOW. Each discipline now carries a `cues` array. Every cue is a TEST he can
perform with a binary result, per the house rule that a doneness cue must never be a sense he has
to have. `confidence` is one of evidence / convention / contested and it is NOT decoration:
"convention" means good coaching practice with no study behind it, said plainly rather than
dressed up. `cuesNote` records what was DROPPED and why, which is the more useful half.
Produced by three research agents and NINE adversarial reviewers, three per discipline, told to
find where the work lied rather than to check it: one verifying every citation exists and says
what is claimed, one testing whether each cue is actually performable, one hunting advice unsafe
at 104.9 kg or contradicting his own plan. It earned its keep: the run drafter called its "Sound"
cue "the strongest injury-reduction finding in the whole set" and the editor dropped it after
fetching the paper. 24 drafted cues became 21 survivors, after rewrites, re-grounding and
three outright deletions.
CORRECTED 2026-08-21, from the per-length lap data rather than from session totals. Three claims
in this file were false, and all three pushed the swim the same way, towards rebuilding something
he can already do:
1. "600 m matches your best unbroken swim of the year, from 2026-06-27." The DISTANCE was right
and the DATE was wrong. 600 m happened twice in one session on 2026-05-22. The 26 June swim
(the watch files it as the 27th, in UTC) topped out at 500 m in 9:35.
2. "Your current best continuous effort is around 3 minutes." It is 11:36.
3. The ladder placed 500 m at weeks 9 to 10. He has passed 500 m on four separate days since
April, and 600 m in May.
The watch resting_time field misses wall stops, so a naive read of the laps is not enough: it
reports a 1,000 m "unbroken" piece on 2026-04-22 that contains a 76-second length sitting next to
a 34-second one. A piece is only counted here if it also survives splitting at any length longer
than 1.5x the median of that piece, which is this file own published test ("any length 4 or more
seconds slower than its predecessor was a rest at the wall") applied backwards over the history.
THE LADDER NO LONGER CARRIES AN OPENING DISTANCE. The lap data says 600 m unbroken, he said 200 m
unassisted, the difference is almost certainly the pull buoy, and the export does not record a
buoy. Asked directly, he did not remember which swims used it. So the rungs are written relative
to a number he measures in one swim, rather than to a constant that would be wrong by up to 400 m
in an unpredictable direction.
THE RUN IS PRESCRIBED IN MINUTES NOW, not metres. The doses are unchanged, still the Bertelsen
3 km arm. On 2026-08-19 he ran 3.1x the week-1 prescription at a speed that was entirely correct
(7.8 km/h, mean HR 113), because the distance target lived on a treadmill console he does not
trust and believes is in miles. A clock cannot be in the wrong unit.

slots.$comment: Where each thing lives in a week. Pool times are his, given 2026-08-15.

morning.name: Morning, before work
morning.what: Run or bike, alternating. About 25 to 45 minutes.
morning.why: The only genuinely new time in the week. Nothing already happening moves to make room.

evening.name: Evening
evening.what: Lift, then swim, as now. Lift first.
evening.why: Unchanged. Held trends favour lifting before the aerobic piece, and this stack is already producing squat progress.

poolTimes.weekdayLate: Weekday late: ~9 pm, the one you normally use

run.title: Run
run.startedFrom: Effectively zero. 3 runs in all of 2025, the last on 2025-08-16. But 65 minutes of walking a day averaged over 60 days, so the engine is there and only the tissue tolerance is missing.
why: Bertelsen 2018 randomised 56 novice runners at BMI 30 to 35, which is your band. The arm that
started at 3 km/week had 2 injuries in 29 people (6.9%). The arm that started at 6 km/week had
5 in 27 (18.5%). Same people, same weeks, double the dose, triple the injuries.
This plan IS the 3 km arm, including its week-1 session verbatim. It will feel absurdly easy.
That is the entire point and the reason it is written down rather than left to feel.

howHard.primary: The talk test. You must be able to say a full sentence out loud without gasping. If you cannot, slow the belt down. There is no version of this plan where running harder is better.
howHard.secondary: If you want a number, keep your heart rate below about 140. Your swims run 130 to 155, so this should feel EASIER than a swim.
howHard.startingSpeed: Set the belt to 8.0 km/h (5.0 mph), then let the talk test move it. Not a guess: on 2026-08-19 you averaged 7.8 km/h at mean heart rate 113, which passes the talk test comfortably. Whatever number it settles at is your number.

weeks.note: Verbatim from the trial arm that got hurt least. The doses did not change on 2026-08-21; only the unit did.
5.7 km a week across three sessions. Reassess here before deciding whether to keep climbing or hold.

rules: Never add more than 10% in a week, and never add distance and speed in the same week.
A missed week means repeat the last week you completed, not jump to where the calendar says.
Any pain that changes how you walk means stop and say so. Shin and knee are the two to watch, and the hip abduction work on lower days is the insurance against exactly those.

cues.name: Step rate
cues.cue: Measure your own step rate, then raise it by 5 percent and hold it there. Step rate, also called cadence, is the number of times a foot lands on the belt in one minute, counting both feet together. Measure it like this: two minutes into a running block, count every time your RIGHT foot lands for 30 seconds, then multiply by 4. Write that number in the log. Your target is that number times 1.05. To hit it you take slightly shorter and quicker steps. You do NOT change the belt speed and you do NOT push harder. Do not use 180 as a target: 180 is a number that comes from runners much faster than you. Re-measure your baseline and recompute the target any time the belt speed changes by 0.5 km/h or more, because step rate moves with speed and your target must move with it. One honest trade, said out loud: 5 percent more steps per minute at the same speed also means 5 percent more foot landings per kilometre. Each landing is softer, but there are more of them, and nobody has studied that trade in runners your size.
cues.test: In the FIRST running block only, after you have said your passage, count your RIGHT foot landings for 30 seconds and multiply by 4. PASS = the number is your target or higher, or no more than 4 below it. FAIL = more than 4 below. On a fail, take shorter and quicker steps at the same belt speed and re-count in the second block. A number ABOVE your target is a pass and needs no action at all. The tolerance of 4 is one miscount's worth and it is my number, not a study's. If your watch has a cadence or step rate field, check it once against your hand count before you trust it: some watches report STRIDES per minute, which is half of steps per minute, so a true 160 would show as 80.
cues.why: Raising step rate is the one form change with a consistent measured effect on how hard your legs get hit. Shorter steps mean a lower peak force between foot and belt (the technical name is vertical ground reaction force) and that force builds more slowly (the loading rate). It is also the only form change you can verify with a number instead of a feeling. The 5 percent is the small end of the range the review covers, deliberately.
cues.grounding: Figueiredo I, Reis e Silva M, Sousa JE. The Influence of Running Cadence on Biomechanics and Injury Prevention: A Systematic Review. Cureus. 2025 Aug 17;17(8):e90322. Fetched https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12440572/ myself. 18 studies, search 2009 to April 2025. Verbatim: "A moderate increase in cadence (typically 5-10%) led to consistent biomechanical improvements, including reduced vertical ground reaction forces, lower loading rates, shorter stride length, and improved lower limb alignment", and cadence change "did not negatively affect metabolic cost". THREE CAVEATS I AM NOT HIDING. (1) The review's own stated limitations: "small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and a predominance of surrogate biomechanical outcomes over clinically meaningful endpoints", plus inconsistent control of running velocity. (2) Cureus is a low-barrier journal, so treat the synthesis as directional. (3) The review does not address heavier or obese runners at all, and I searched separately and found no study of step-rate manipulation at BMI 30 to 35. For why 180 is not his number: Leacox A, Fashingbauer L, Ferguson T, Zajakowski A, Baum B, Reinking M. The Effect of Running Speed on Cadence and Running Kinetics. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2025;20(7):957-963, fetched at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12222555/. n=30 (19M, 11F, ages 21-49), inclusion was "running at least 15 miles per week for one year", and the paper calls them EXPERIENCED runners, not recreational. Cadence rose 169.2, 169.9, 170.5, 172.3, 174.3, 175.9, 177.9 steps/min across 2.68 m/s (10 min/mile) to 3.83 m/s (7 min/mile). Eight of the 30 changed by less than 4 steps/min across that whole range, which is why the target has to come off his own baseline. WHAT I WILL NOT CLAIM: the paper says nothing about speeds below 2.68 m/s, nothing about novices, and its introduction actually cites prior work linking LOWER cadence to higher injury risk (Kliethermes 2021, Luedke 2016). So I assert only that 180 is not a universal floor, and I have deleted the earlier draft's "150s or low 160s is normal at his pace" band as an unsourced extrapolation below the tested range.

cues.name: One change only
cues.cue: Step rate is the only thing about your running form you deliberately change on this plan. Whatever part of your foot hits the belt first, leave it alone. That is called your footstrike: heel first is a rearfoot strike, ball of the foot first is a forefoot strike, flat is a midfoot strike. Most beginners land heel first. If that is you, you keep it. You also do not work on posture, arm swing, leaning forward, breathing rhythm, or landing quietly. If an app, a video, a coach or a friend tells you your footstrike is wrong, the answer is no. The one thing that overrides all of this is pain: pain that changes the way you walk means stop the session, not change your form.
cues.test: Before you press Start, write one line in the log: the single form thing you are working on today. PASS = the line reads "step rate" and nothing else is on it. FAIL = anything else appears on that line, in which case cross it out and start the session with step rate only.
cues.why: Switching a heel striker onto the forefoot moves load off the knee and onto the calf and Achilles tendon, which at 104.9 kg is the tissue least prepared to take it, and it makes running immediately harder at the same speed. There is no prospective evidence that the switch prevents injury. The wider rule matters for a second reason: if you change two things at once and something starts hurting, you cannot tell which one did it.
cues.grounding: Anderson LM, Bonanno DR, Hart HF, Barton CJ. What are the Benefits and Risks Associated with Changing Foot Strike Pattern During Running? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Injury, Running Economy, and Biomechanics. Sports Med. 2020;50(5):885-917. Fetched at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=31823338&rettype=abstract&retmode=text. 53 studies. Non-rearfoot striking is only RETROSPECTIVELY associated with lower reported injury rates. Running economy did not differ between habitual patterns and got worse when rearfoot strikers switched. Non-rearfoot running showed lower vertical loading rate but increased ankle plantarflexor loading (the calf and Achilles). Stated conclusion: "Changing strike pattern cannot be recommended for an uninjured RFS runner." THE PACKAGING IS CONVENTION: the footstrike prohibition is evidence-based, but the one-change-at-a-time rule and the written log line are coaching practice with no study behind them, which is why this row is tagged convention rather than evidence.

cues.name: Incline zero
cues.cue: Set the console incline to 0.0 percent and keep it at 0.0 for the entire session, walks and runs alike. Ignore the widely repeated advice to run treadmills at 1 percent.
cues.test: Two looks, both must read 0.0. (1) Before you press Start, the incline readout says 0.0. If it says anything else, press incline down until it does. (2) During the 200 m walk between the two running blocks, look again. PASS = both looks show 0.0. FAIL = either look shows anything else, in which case set it back to 0.0 and write it in the log, because a console programme that moves the incline on its own will do it again next time.
cues.why: The 1 percent habit is a real study applied outside the conditions it tested. It exists to make the energy cost of treadmill running match the energy cost of running OUTDOORS, for trained runners at racing speeds. Matching outdoor energy cost is not one of your goals, and your speed is below anything that study measured. Incline adds work for no stated reason, and the design principle of week one is that it should feel absurdly easy.
cues.grounding: Jones AM, Doust JH. A 1% treadmill grade most accurately reflects the energetic cost of outdoor running. J Sports Sci. 1996;14(4):321-327. Fetched at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=8887211&rettype=abstract&retmode=text. NINE trained male runners, six speeds (2.92, 3.33, 3.75, 4.17, 4.58, 5.0 m/s, which is 10.5 to 18.0 km/h), grades of 0, 1, 2 and 3 percent plus level road. At the TWO SLOWEST speeds, outdoor running matched both the 0 percent and the 1 percent treadmill conditions; the 1 percent recommendation was driven by 3.75 m/s and faster. His 7.0 km/h is 1.94 m/s, below the slowest speed the paper ever tested. This is a 1996 paper cited deliberately because it is the sole origin of the claim, and I found no replication.

cues.name: Belt speed
cues.cue: Run the running blocks with both hands off the handrails, arms free at your sides. Grabbing a rail because you stumbled or lost your balance is ALWAYS the right move and is never a failure. Holding a rail to keep up with the belt is different, and it means the belt is too fast. The belt speed is found by testing, not chosen in advance, because 7.0 km/h is a guess that nobody sourced.
cues.test: Sessions 1 and 2 are familiarisation: rail grabs do not count at all while you learn a moving belt. From session 3 onward, PASS = you finished both running blocks without holding a rail to keep up. A grab you let go of within about two steps is a balance grab and is always a pass. FAIL = you were still holding after two steps, or you were holding when the block ended. On a fail, the next session runs 0.5 km/h slower. HARD LIMITS, and these override every other test in this set: a maximum of ONE 0.5 km/h reduction per session no matter how many tests you failed, and never below 6.0 km/h. If you reach 6.0 km/h and are still failing, stop dropping the belt, write it in the log, and the plan gets revisited instead.
cues.why: Holding the rails takes weight off your legs and does your balancing for you, so a speed you can hold while gripping is not a speed you are actually running. It also corrupts your other gauge: leaning on the rails lowers your heart rate and makes talking easier, so both the passage and the watch will read easier than the truth. Two honest caveats. In week one a rail grab is at least as likely to be unfamiliarity with a moving belt as it is to be speed, which is why the first two sessions do not count. And the 6.0 km/h floor exists because a belt driven low enough stops being running and becomes walking, at which point you are no longer doing the protocol the low injury number came from.
cues.grounding: CONVENTION. I searched specifically for evidence on handrail use during running and found only stroke rehabilitation and older-adult inclined-walking work, which does not transfer to a healthy adult jogging, so I am not citing it. The 0.5 km/h step, the two-step rule, the one-drop cap and the 6.0 km/h floor are all my numbers. What IS sourced is that the plan's 7.0 km/h has no origin: Bertelsen ML, Hansen M, Rasmussen S, Nielsen RO, Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2018;13(6):943-955 (fetched at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/) prescribed distance and an intensity instruction only, on "a self-chosen route" outdoors. Relevant from the same research group: Bertelsen et al, How Do Novice Runners With Different Body Mass Indexes Begin a Self-chosen Running Regime? J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2018;48(11):873-877 (fetched at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=29932876&rettype=abstract&retmode=text) found obese novice runners self-selected a pace 1.7 km/h SLOWER than normal-weight novices (95% CI -2.0 to -1.4). So a starting speed below 7.0 would be unremarkable.

cues.name: The passage
cues.cue: Pick about 30 words you know by heart, write them down once, and use the SAME words every session forever. Say them out loud at normal speaking volume to gauge how hard you are working. You have two gauges, the passage and the watch, and the rule is that whichever one is stricter wins. If the passage fails, you slow down even if the watch reads under 140. If the watch reads over 140, you slow down even if the words came out fine. There is no situation in which one gauge gives you permission to ignore the other.
cues.test: Say the passage out loud when the console distance readout shows you are halfway through a running block, so 250 m into a 500 m block. PASS = you get all the words out with at most one break to breathe, AND your watch reads 140 or below. If you are unsure whether you broke to breathe, count it as a break. FAIL = two or more breaks, or you cannot finish the words, or the watch reads above 140. On any fail, drop the belt 0.5 km/h immediately and start the next session at the lower speed. This drop is the same single drop as the belt speed cue, capped at one per session, floor 6.0 km/h.
cues.why: The plan gives two intensity gauges and never says which wins when they disagree, and they will disagree. Setting the stricter one as the winner is the safe resolution: it means an inaccurate wrist heart rate can only ever make you go easier, never harder. Fixing the words matters because an improvised sentence gets shorter as you tire, so the test quietly gets easier exactly when you need it to hold. A fixed passage is also what the validation studies used.
cues.grounding: THREE SOURCES, ALL FETCHED, ALL WITH POPULATION PROBLEMS I AM NAMING. (1) The primacy of a talk-based gauge in his own protocol: Bertelsen 2018, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/, instructed participants only to "run with a moderate intensity i.e. being able to converse without breathlessness". No heart rate, no pace, so the words are the trial's gauge and the 140 is not. (2) Vieira AM et al. Application and Measurement Properties of the Talk Test in Cardiopulmonary Patients: A Systematic Review. Rev Cardiovasc Med. 2022;23(7):225, fetched at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11266803/. 10 studies, 426 subjects (not "roughly 414 to 426", that hedge was wrong). Workload, oxygen uptake and heart rate at the last positive talk-test stage were not different from the same measures at the first ventilatory threshold; correlations 0.37 to 0.83. Protocols used standardised 30-word passages. CONTESTED: more than 99 percent of subjects had cardiovascular disease and 60 percent of protocols used a cycle ergometer, and the authors themselves flag missing evidence on "applicability of the talk test in a more heterogeneous population". (3) For a healthy population on a treadmill: Kwon Y, Nam KS, Chang JS, Kang KW. Comparison of cardiorespiratory responses between treadmill and bicycle ergometer exercise. J Exerc Rehabil. 2025;21(3):114-123, fetched at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12214955/. 22 healthy adults (17M, 5F, mean age 26.6), reciting the 31-word Pledge of Allegiance at each stage; talk-test stage correlated with heart rate r=0.869, RPE r=0.920, METs r=0.893, all P<0.001, on the treadmill. Small, young, and a graded maximal test rather than a steady jog, so supporting rather than decisive. THE 140 ITSELF HAS NO SOURCE anywhere in the plan and I could not find one; treat it as a convention ceiling.

cues.name: Stopping and the walks
cues.cue: The walk segments are part of the training, not a rest, so keep walking through them with both feet on the moving belt. Do not stop the belt to rest and do not stand on the side rails to catch your breath. Stopping for a reason other than rest is a completely different thing and is always correct: pain that changes the way you walk, dizziness, chest pain, or anything that feels wrong means you stop, and that is never scored as a failure of anything.
cues.test: Three checks. (1) BEFORE you press Start, the red safety clip is clipped to your shirt and its key is in the console. PASS = you can see the cord running from your shirt to the machine. If the machine has no clip, use a different machine. (2) During the 500 m and 200 m walk segments, both feet stay on the moving belt and you keep walking. Set the walk speed at a pace where you could say your whole passage with no breaks at all. PASS = the belt never stopped and you never stood on the side rails to catch your breath. FAIL = either of those, and the next session runs 0.5 km/h slower, sharing the one-drop-per-session cap. (3) A deliberate stop for pain, dizziness or anything wrong is a PASS. Pull the clip, stop, write what happened in the log, and no speed penalty follows.
cues.why: The 3 km per week arm of the trial your week one is copied from had 6.9 percent injured against 18.5 percent in the arm that ran double, and its pauses were spent walking, not standing. If you turn the walks into standing rests you are no longer running the protocol that produced the low number. The safety clip and the never-punish-a-stop rule are here because the earlier draft of these cues told you never to stop the belt and scored a rail grab as a failure, which between them would have removed every way of aborting safely from a moving belt at 104.9 kg. That was wrong and it is fixed.
cues.grounding: Bertelsen ML, Hansen M, Rasmussen S, Nielsen RO. The Start-to-Run Distance and Running-Related Injury Among Obese Novice Runners: A Randomized Trial. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2018;13(6):943-955. I fetched the full text twice at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/. Verbatim: "The running distance in both programs was split up into shorter intervals with walking at an easy/comfortable pace in the pauses between each interval." Inclusion BMI 30-35, no previous running experience (less than 10 km combined in the last year), self-chosen outdoor route. Injuries: 2 of 29 (6.9 percent) in the 3 km arm, 5 of 27 (18.5 percent) in the 6 km arm. Week 1 of the 3 km arm is 500 m walk, 500 m run, 200 m walk, 500 m run, three sessions. LABELLED CONVENTION because the trial never compared walking against standing, it only walked. The earlier draft's 5.0 km/h minimum walk speed is DELETED: it was my invention, it is stricter than "easy/comfortable", and a brisk forced walk eats the recovery the pause exists for. The safety clip check is convention too: I searched for evidence and found only US Consumer Product Safety Commission injury counts reported through news outlets and equipment blogs, and I will not cite a blog for a number.

cues.name: Shoes
cues.cue: Choose running shoes on fit first, using the test below. If two pairs both pass the fit test, take the softer and more cushioned one. Do not pay extra for anything sold as stability or motion control, and do not trust a shoe because the box says it is for heavier runners. The one large trial on this question changed only how soft the foam was and nothing else, so it says nothing whatsoever about stability or motion control, and it cannot tell you whether cushioning protects a man your size.
cues.test: Do this late in the day, in the socks you will run in. Pull the insole out of the shoe first. The insole is the loose flat liner you can lift out from inside. Put it on the floor and stand on it. Three checks, all three must pass. (1) Look down at the gap in front of your longest toe, which is not always the big toe. PASS = the insole extends at least a thumb width past the end of it. (2) Look at the sides of the insole. PASS = no part of your foot hangs over the edge anywhere. (3) Put the insole back, lace the shoe and walk 20 steps. The heel cup is the stiff cup at the back of the shoe that wraps around your heel. PASS = your heel stays down inside it and does not lift away as you step. Any one fail means it is the wrong shoe, whatever the price, the brand or the review says.
cues.why: The trial split its runners at the middle of their own body-mass range, 78.2 kg for men. At 104.9 kg you sit above even the heavier half, so the trial does not really cover you. In that heavier half the harder shoe still pointed the wrong way, about 23 percent more injury risk, but the range around that number ran from 25 percent lower to roughly double, so it could easily be chance. The honest reading is that the question is unsettled for a man your size, not that cushioning is irrelevant. Fit is where beginners actually get hurt in month one: a shoe that is too short or too narrow produces black toenails and forefoot pain inside a few weeks.
cues.grounding: Malisoux L, Delattre N, Urhausen A, Theisen D. Shoe Cushioning Influences the Running Injury Risk According to Body Mass: A Randomized Controlled Trial Involving 848 Recreational Runners. Am J Sports Med. 2020;48(2):473-480. Fetched at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=31877062&rettype=abstract&retmode=text. 848 healthy recreational runners randomised to two prototypes differing only in cushioning stiffness (soft 61.3 +/- 2.7 N/mm, hard 94.9 +/- 5.9 N/mm). Overall the hard shoe carried higher injury risk, subhazard ratio 1.52 (95% CI 1.07-2.16). Split at median body mass (78.2 kg men, 62.8 kg women): lighter group 1.80 (1.09-2.98), heavier group 1.23 (0.75-2.03). Stated conclusion: "the relative protective effect of greater shoe cushioning was found only in lighter runners." CONTESTED FOR HIM, in both directions. The heavier subgroup's confidence interval contains the lighter group's 1.80, so the trial is underpowered there rather than showing no effect, and the earlier draft's instruction to "ignore every cushioning claim" read absence of evidence as evidence of absence and could have pushed him toward the harder shoe, the one direction with no support at all. SEPARATELY: the three fit checks are pure CONVENTION with no study behind them. They are in this row because they are the actionable part, not because the trial supports them.

run.cuesNote:
EVERY CITATION IN THE FINAL SET WAS FETCHED BY ME IN THIS PASS, NOT INHERITED. URLs are in each grounding field. Nothing is quoted from memory.

WHAT I DROPPED, AND WHY.

1. THE "SOUND" CUE. Dropped entirely. This is the biggest change and it inverts the draft's own ranking, which called it "the strongest injury-reduction finding in the whole set". I fetched Phan X, Grisbrook TL, Wernli K, Stearne SM, Davey P, Ng L. Running quietly reduces ground reaction force and vertical loading rate and alters foot strike technique. J Sports Sci. 2017;35(16):1636-1642, at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=27594087&rettype=abstract&retmode=text. Two findings kill the cue. First, verbatim: "Simple linear regressions revealed no significant relationships between impact sound and peak vGRF in the normal and quiet conditions and vertical loading rate in the normal condition", and the authors conclude "quieter impact sound is not directly associated with a lower peak vGRF or vertical loading rate". So the noise he would be listening to is not a valid proxy for the force. Second, verbatim: "During the normal running condition, 15.4% of participants utilised a non-rearfoot strike technique compared to 76.9% in the quiet condition, which was corroborated by an increased ankle plantarflexion angle at initial contact." Roughly three runners in four converted to landing on the forefoot. That is precisely the conversion Anderson 2020 says cannot be recommended for an uninjured heel striker because it increases ankle plantarflexor loading, and at 104.9 kg the calf and Achilles are the tissue least able to absorb it. The instruction "do not think about which part of your foot lands" does not prevent the switch, it only removes the chance of noticing it. The cue was also unmeasurable in practice (pass judged against whatever a given treadmill's motor sounds like) and at his mass probably unpassable, with an open-ended remedy loop whose only remaining strategy is to land on the toes. The set kept the paper warning against the outcome and prescribed the cue that reliably produces it.

2. THE FOOTSTRIKE VIDEO TEST. Dropped. It put an unsecured phone on the side rail of a running treadmill next to a moving belt, and by the cue's own logic no video result changed any action, so it was a physical risk taken to generate a log entry. Standard phone video at 30 frames per second also cannot reliably resolve a touchdown that lasts about a quarter of a second. The substance survives as a prohibition inside "One change only".

3. THE ABSOLUTE "NEVER STOP THE BELT" AND "RAIL GRAB = FAIL" RULES. Dropped. Between them they removed both abort routes from a first-time treadmill user at 104.9 kg, and scoring a stop as a failure directly contradicts the plan's own rule that pain changing how he walks means stop. Replaced with: stopping for pain, dizziness or anything wrong is always a PASS with no penalty; a balance grab is always correct; only holding on to keep up with the belt counts against him. The safety clip is now a pre-start check, which the plan did not mention at all.

4. THE THREE INDEPENDENT 0.5 km/h SPEED DROPS. Dropped as written. Three separate cues each dropped the belt with no floor and no interaction rule, so a bad session could take 7.0 to 5.5 km/h and turn the run blocks into walking. Replaced with one drop per session maximum, shared across all tests, and a 6.0 km/h floor below which the plan gets revisited rather than the belt. The floor and the cap are my numbers, labelled as such.

5. THE 5.0 km/h WALK FLOOR. Dropped. It was invented, it is stricter than Bertelsen's actual instruction ("walking at an easy/comfortable pace in the pauses"), and a brisk forced walk only 2.0 km/h below his running speed eats the recovery the pause exists for. Replaced with a pace at which the passage comes out with no breaks at all.

6. THE CADENCE BAND "150s OR LOW 160s IS NORMAL AT HIS PACE". Dropped as an unsourced extrapolation presented under a citation. Leacox 2025's slowest condition is 2.68 m/s; his 7.0 km/h is 1.94 m/s, 27 percent slower than anything measured. The draft convicted the 1 percent incline rule for exactly this error one cue later. The myth-bust does not need the band and survives without it.

7. "THE 10 PERCENT WEEKLY RULE IS MORE AGGRESSIVE THAN THE TRIAL." Dropped because it is FALSE, and writing it into the evidence file would have planted a false correction. I fetched Table 1 twice. The 3 km arm is not three identical sessions per week: weeks 1 and 2 are uniform (1.0 km and 1.1 km of running per session), but weeks 3 and 4 vary session to session, and week 4 ends with a session containing a single continuous 1000 m run, double week one's longest. Weekly running totals are 3.0, 3.3, about 3.6 and 4.0 km. The paper's own text says "The running distance was increased by ~10% per week." My two fetches of the same table differed slightly on one week-3 session, so I am not asserting the week-3 total to two decimal places; what is confirmed twice is that week 4 exceeds week 3 and the trial escalated roughly 10 percent weekly. THE REAL CAUTION IS DIFFERENT AND STILL WORTH RECORDING: the trial ran four weeks. Applying a clean 10 percent every week for months is an extrapolation past anything it measured.

8. TWO UNSOURCED WRIST HEART-RATE FIGURES. Dropped from the notes: "mean absolute percentage error of 3.3 to 6.2 percent" and "13 to 23 percent error in some devices during trail running". I searched and could not attach either to a paper I read. The underlying meta-analysis does exist (Validity of Wrist-Worn photoplethysmography devices to measure heart rate: a systematic review and meta-analysis, J Sports Sci 2020;38(17), 44 articles, 738 effect sizes, 15 brands), but I did not verify its per-activity numbers, so none appear here. The decision not to write a wrist heart-rate cue now rests on something better: the passage cue sets the stricter gauge as the winner, so any device error can only make him go easier.

9. NO CUE WRITTEN FOR: breathing pattern, arm swing, trunk lean, "run tall", posture, or overstriding. Nothing citable. On overstriding specifically, Baker et al. Sci Rep. 2024;14:6347 states that recent systematic reviews show a lack of consensus on the relationship between braking force and injury, and every popular guide to detecting it that I found was a blog with no measurement behind it. Usefully, the same work found overstriding falls as stride frequency rises, which is another reason step rate is the lever.

MYTHS I AM CONFIDENT ENOUGH TO NAME.

A. "AIM FOR 180 STEPS PER MINUTE." Not his number, and the target should never be an absolute. Leacox 2025 measured EXPERIENCED runners (inclusion: 15 miles a week for a year) at 169.2 steps/min at 10 min/mile rising to 177.9 at 7 min/mile. Every one of those speeds is faster than his 7.0 km/h. Eight of thirty barely changed cadence across the whole range. Correction to the draft, which the skeptics caught and which I confirmed in the paper: those participants are experienced runners, not "recreational". Caveat I am keeping visible: the same paper's introduction cites prior work linking lower cadence to higher injury risk, so "180 is not universal" is the claim, not "low cadence is fine".

B. "SET THE TREADMILL TO 1 PERCENT." A real 1996 study on nine trained men at 10.5 to 18.0 km/h, applied far outside its range. At the two slowest speeds it tested, 0 percent matched outdoor running just as well as 1 percent. He runs slower than the slowest speed in the paper. I found no replication.

C. "HEEL STRIKING IS BAD, LAND ON YOUR FOREFOOT." Anderson 2020, 53 studies: prospective injury evidence is lacking, economy gets worse on an acute switch, ankle plantarflexor loading increases, and the authors state the change cannot be recommended for an uninjured rearfoot striker.

D. "RUN QUIETLY AND YOU WILL LAND SOFTER." The sound itself does not track the force (Phan 2017, no significant relationship), and the instruction converts about three runners in four to a forefoot landing. For him this is not merely unsupported, it is the mechanism of the thing cue 2 forbids.

E. "HEAVY RUNNERS NEED MAXIMUM CUSHIONING", AND ITS OPPOSITE. The one large RCT found the protective effect of soft cushioning only in the lighter half of its sample. But the heavier subgroup was underpowered, not null, so "ignore cushioning" is equally wrong. Unsettled at his mass.

WHAT THE PLAN GETS WRONG OR LEAVES OPEN.

a) THE 7.0 km/h BELT SPEED HAS NO SOURCE. Bertelsen prescribed distance and a talk-based intensity instruction only, outdoors, on a self-chosen route at a self-chosen speed. In the same research group's companion paper, obese novices self-selected 1.7 km/h slower than normal-weight novices (95% CI -2.0 to -1.4 km/h). The belt speed cue exists so he finds his number instead of inheriting a guess.

b) THIS IS A TREADMILL PLAN BUILT ON A NON-TREADMILL TRIAL. Now cited rather than hedged. Miller JR, Van Hooren B, Bishop C, Buckley JD, Willy RW, Fuller JT. Sports Med. 2019;49:763-782, doi 10.1007/s40279-019-01087-9, fetched at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=30847825&rettype=abstract&retmode=text, states verbatim: "HR and RPE during motorised treadmill running were higher at faster submaximal speeds and lower at slower submaximal speeds than during overground running." At his slow speed the treadmill will read easier than the outdoor equivalent, which matters if the runs ever move outside.

c) "HEART RATE UNDER ABOUT 140" HAS NO SOURCE and conflicts with the talk test sitting beside it. I searched and found no origin for the 140. The passage cue resolves the conflict in the safe direction (stricter gauge wins, both directions written out), which also protects the plan's architecture: hard aerobic work is supposed to live on the bike at 150 to 165 so the running stays short and easy. A run habitually cleared at 155 by the talk test alone would collapse the two sessions into one zone. The evidence file should either give the 140 an origin or mark it convention.

d) NO CADENCE EVIDENCE EXISTS AT BMI 30 TO 35. I searched for it directly. Everything in the cadence literature is normal-BMI runners, and the Bertelsen trial that supplies his week one gave no technique instruction at all. The step-rate cue is the best-supported thing in the set and it is still an extrapolation to his body. It also raises total foot landings per kilometre by about 5 percent, a trade no source addresses, which is why the cue says so out loud.

e) THE BEST INJURY EVIDENCE IN THIS FIELD IS NOT AVAILABLE TO HIM. Chan et al. AJSM 2018 randomised 320 novice runners and cut 12-month injury from 38 percent to 16 percent (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.25-0.59), but the intervention was real-time VISUAL feedback of vertical impact peak on a force-instrumented treadmill, not sound and not cadence. No home substitute has been shown to reproduce it. I removed that trial from the set rather than borrow its result for a cue it did not test.

f) SESSION LOAD. At 7.0 km/h a 500 m run block lasts about 4 minutes 17 seconds, so the cues have to be sequenced rather than stacked. As written: pre-start (clip, incline, log line), walk, block one (passage at the 250 m mark, then the 30-second step count), the 200 m walk (second incline glance), block two (passage at the 250 m mark). Nothing is asked of him twice at once.

beltSettings.theUnitTest: Read the speed display once, on the first run. Near 8 means km/h, so check the km figure below. Near 5 means miles. Settled for good.
beltSettings.whyBothUnits: Both units printed, because you have said you think the console is in miles.

whyTheClockNotTheConsole: Minutes, not metres. On 2026-08-19 you ran 3,121 m against a 500 m prescription, 3.1 times it, at
a speed that was fine: 7.8 km/h, mean heart rate 113. The distance ran away because the target
lived on a console you cannot read. A clock cannot be in the wrong unit. The km and miles below
are an after-the-fact check, and when they disagree the clock wins.

bike.title: Bike
why: This answers 'I don't know what to do on them', and the bike earns its place for one specific
reason. Wilson 2012 is the only meta-analysis that separates the endurance MODALITY: running,
but NOT cycling, produced significant decrements in strength and hypertrophy.
So the bike is where hard aerobic work can go for free, which is exactly what lets the running
stay short and easy. It is not filler. It is the thing protecting both other goals.

protocol.name: Norwegian 4x4
protocol.structure: 10 min easy · then 4 rounds of [4 min hard, 3 min easy] · then 5 min easy
protocol.shortVersion: If the morning is tight: 5 min easy · 3 rounds of [4 min hard, 3 min easy] · 5 min easy. 31 minutes.
protocol.evidenceNote: The 4x4 itself is well established and has been replicated on cycling as well as running. The commonly quoted 10 to 15% VO2max improvement in untrained adults comes from secondary summaries rather than a primary paper read end to end, so treat the protocol as sourced and that percentage as indicative.

howHard.hardPiece: By the end of each 4 minutes you should only be able to get out two or three words at a time. Not a sprint: a sprint dies at 90 seconds and this has to last 4 minutes. Pick a resistance you could hold for 5 minutes but would not want to.
howHard.heartRate: Aim to finish each hard piece somewhere around 150 to 165. Your highest recorded swim heart rate is 175, so that band is derived from what your watch has actually seen, not from a formula.
howHard.easyPiece: Genuinely easy. Keep pedalling, get your breath fully back before the next one.

rules: Same morning slot as the run, alternating: run, bike, run, run, bike across a fortnight.
Never on the morning before a heavy lower day if you can avoid it.
The first two sessions, deliberately undercook the hard pieces. You have not done intervals and the first honest 4 minutes is a shock.

cues.name: Set the seat, then be able to reproduce it
cues.cue: A gym bike is set by whoever used it last, so the seat height is something you re-set every visit, not something you solve once. Do it before you pedal. Sit on the seat. Put your HEEL on the pedal, not the ball of your foot. Turn the pedals slowly until that pedal is at its lowest point, straight down under you, so the crank (the metal arm the pedal bolts onto) points at the floor. At that point the leg should be straight with the heel still touching, without you leaning to that side to reach. Then slide the foot forward so the pedal sits under the ball of your foot, the pad behind your big toe. That slide is what leaves a small bend in the knee at the bottom of each stroke. Now write the setting down: the number on the seat post (the vertical tube the seat sits on, which slides up and down inside the frame), or if it has no numbers, the count of holes or notches from the bottom. Next week you set that number first and skip the test. Precision matters less than you think, repeatability matters more: being a centimetre off changes almost nothing, being on a different setting every week means none of your resistance numbers compare.
cues.test: Two looks, both straight down at your own leg, no mirror and no helper. STATIC, before pedalling: heel on the pedal at its lowest point. Is the leg straight without you leaning toward that side? Knee still visibly bent, raise one setting. Cannot reach unless you lean or point your toes down, lower one setting. DYNAMIC, in the first minute of the warm-up with the ball of your foot on the pedal: look down at that knee each time the foot reaches the bottom. Is there a small visible bend in it every single time, never snapping dead straight? Yes, done, leave it. Knee locking straight at the bottom, or toes pointing down to keep contact, lower one setting and look again.
cues.why: The only thing the review calls strong evidence is judging the knee angle while pedalling, which is what the dynamic half of the test does. The heel-on-pedal method itself is workshop convention with no validation behind it, and it is here only because it lands you close, which the same review says is close enough.
cues.grounding: Bini R, Priego-Quesada J. "Methods to determine saddle height in cycling and implications of changes in saddle height in performance and injury risk: A systematic review." Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022;40(4):386-400. DOI 10.1080/02640414.2021.1994727, PMID 34706617. 29,398 records screened, 41 studies included. Verbatim from the abstract I fetched: "Strong evidence suggests that saddle height should be configured using dynamic measurements of the knee angle"; "moderate evidence suggests that changes in saddle height less than 4% of the leg length results in trivial to small changes in lower limb loads, and no effect on oxygen uptake and efficiency"; "there is limited evidence on the effects from changes in saddle height on supramaximal cycling performance or injury risk". Publisher full text 403s, so I read the record via the Europe PMC REST API (URL below). Secondary, also fetched: Bing, Zhang, Wei & Zhang, Front Sports Act Living 2025 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483900/) restates a 25-35 degree knee angle at bottom dead centre and reports static and dynamic knee angles differing by 8.2 +/- 5 degrees. That degree figure is background in that paper, not something it tested, which is why no degree number appears in the cue text.

cues.name: Make the two numbers readable before you start
cues.cue: Every rule below is a glance at two numbers at a named second: your live heart rate, and how long you are into the CURRENT piece. Set both up before the first pedal stroke. On the watch, start a workout that shows heart rate as a number on the screen. The bike console counts total elapsed time for the whole session, so it can never tell you that you are two minutes into interval three. The watch can: press the lap button at the start of every 4 minute effort and again at the start of every 3 minute recovery, so the lap timer always shows time inside the piece you are in. If your watch cannot do laps, set a repeating countdown on your phone, 4 minutes then 3 minutes, and read the countdown instead.
cues.test: Sitting on the bike, before you start: can you see a heart rate number in beats per minute AND a timer you can reset to zero, at the same time, without pressing more than one button? If no, fix it now, before the warm-up. Doing arithmetic on the console's total time at 160 beats per minute is not a thing that happens.
cues.why: Eight of the checks in this list are unperformable without a live heart rate and interval-relative time, and nothing in the plan establishes either. This is not evidence-based, it is the difference between a rule you can follow and a rule you cannot.
cues.grounding: CONVENTION

cues.name: Warm up to a heart-rate number, and still finish on time
cues.cue: The 10 easy minutes have a target, not just a duration. Pedal hard enough that your heart rate reads 105 to 123 by minute 8, and hold it to minute 10. For the 3 minute recoveries between efforts, 88 to 123 is fine, and note that is a WIDER band than the warm-up, not the same one. The published protocol asks for 60 to 70 percent of peak heart rate in the warm-up and 50 to 70 percent in the recoveries; applied to 175 that gives those two bands. Whatever the number says at minute 8, the warm-up ends at minute 10 and interval 1 starts. Do not extend it. The session is 43 minutes and it stays 43 minutes.
cues.test: One look at the watch at minute 8 of the warm-up. Heart rate 105 to 123: hold this resistance and start interval 1 at minute 10. Under 105: add one resistance level, and still start at minute 10. Over 123: drop one level. Then during each 3 minute recovery, one look at 2:00 into it. Above 123: drop one level. Below 88: add one level.
cues.why: The plan currently says "easy", which is a feeling, and the protocol puts percentages on it. The honest gap: HRpeak means a peak from a maximal test, and 175 is just the highest number his watch has happened to record in submaximal training by a man who has never made a maximal effort, so his real maximum is probably higher and these bands are probably slightly low. That is the safe direction to be wrong in for week one, and it is not a reason to go looking for the real number.
cues.grounding: Tjonna et al., the EX-MET study protocol, BMC Public Health 2018, a randomised multicentre trial in adults with metabolic syndrome, performed on "cycle or treadmill ergometer (self-selected)". Its 4x4 arm, verbatim: "10-min warm-up" at "60-70% peak heart rate (HRpeak)", "4 x 4 min" at "85-95% HRpeak" with target heart rate "reached within two minutes", "3 min of active recovery at 50-70% HRpeak", "3-min cool-down at 60-70% peak heart rate", 3 times per week, 38 minutes per session. I checked specifically: the protocol paper never defines how HRpeak was measured.

cues.name: Hold the RPM, change the resistance
cues.cue: Cadence means how many complete circles one foot makes in a minute. The console shows it as RPM, sometimes labelled cadence. Pick a number near 80 and keep it there all session, hard minutes and easy ones alike. When the session needs to be harder or easier you change the RESISTANCE LEVEL, never the RPM. One variable, and the RPM is the one you hold still, so that "level 9 for four minutes" means the same thing next Tuesday as it did this Tuesday. The exact number is not sacred: nothing bad happens at 75 or at 85. If the console shows no RPM at all, count one foot's circles for 15 seconds and multiply by four (20 circles in 15 seconds is 80 RPM), do that once during the warm-up so you know what it feels like at that resistance, and then run the whole session on the resistance rule alone.
cues.test: Look at the RPM readout once per effort, at 2:00, in the same glance as the heart rate, and not before. Below 70: drop one resistance level, and that is the only change you make this interval. Above 95: add one level. Between 70 and 95: leave it alone. That is the entire cadence rule for the session.
cues.why: The real reason is bookkeeping, not physiology: holding cadence makes resistance the only thing that moves, so the numbers you write down mean something a week later. There is a second reason that is arithmetic rather than a study: power equals force times pedal speed, so at the same watts a slower stroke means more force per push. I went looking for evidence that a particular cadence protects the knee and it is mixed, so I did not build the cue on it. The one paper I fetched supporting it (Ebbecke, Hansen, Nackel, Viellehner & Potthast, ISB Stockholm 2025 conference abstract, https://fis.dshs-koeln.de/en/publications/knee-joint-loading-during-cycling-should-osteoarthritis-patients-/) tested 12 male ACTIVE cyclists with diagnosed knee osteoarthritis, age 57.3 +/- 7.9, BMI 25.7 +/- 2.9, at 157 to 261 W, and states verbatim "The only exceptions were KAMpeak at 157 W and 210 W between 60 and 80 rpm", so at the low power outputs a beginner actually rides, 60 to 80 rpm made no significant difference to peak knee load. Wrong age, wrong BMI, joint disease he does not have, powers above what he will hold, and not peer reviewed.
cues.grounding: CONVENTION

cues.name: Do not touch the resistance before 2:00
cues.cue: Set the resistance in the first 15 seconds of each 4 minute effort and then leave it completely alone until 2:00. At 30 and 60 seconds the watch will look too low. That is normal: on a bike the heart rate takes over a minute to arrive, and the published protocol expects the target to be reached "within two minutes". Cranking the resistance at 40 seconds because the watch says 128 is the single most likely way a first interval session goes wrong. At 2:00 you make one decision, in a fixed order, cadence first and then heart rate, and then you ride out the last two minutes. Also expect the resistance level to be LOWER in interval 4 than in interval 1. That is normal and it is not you failing, the effort needed to produce a given heart rate falls as the session goes on. Write down the level you finished each effort on, so next week starts from real numbers.
cues.test: At 2:00 into each 4 minute effort, one look, two readouts, at most one change. (1) RPM below 70? Drop one resistance level and stop there, no heart rate check this interval. (2) Otherwise, heart rate 150 to 165: change nothing. Under 150: add one level. Over 165: drop one level. No further changes until the next effort, with two standing overrides that beat this rule at any second: if you have to come off the seat to turn the pedals, drop a level, and if a stop rule fires, stop. The session succeeded if all four efforts ended with heart rate between 150 and 165. Whether the resistance number went up, down, or nowhere is not part of that test.
cues.why: The load-bearing fact, that heart rate lags well over a minute on a bike, is sourced twice and is the whole reason the 2:00 checkpoint exists. The single-decision design and the falling-number reassurance are my convention layered on top of that fact, not findings, and the falling number is deliberately not a success criterion because a session where all four efforts landed in the band is a good session whatever the resistance did.
cues.grounding: Two papers, both fetched. (1) Tjonna et al., EX-MET protocol, BMC Public Health 2018, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5879994/: the 4x4 arm specifies the interval target heart rate is "reached within two minutes". (2) Acala JJ, Roche-Willis D, Astorino TA. "Characterizing the Heart Rate Response to the 4 x 4 Interval Exercise Protocol." Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2020;17(14):5103. 39 healthy ACTIVE adults (20 M, 19 F, age 26.0 +/- 6.1, body mass 72.1 +/- 10.8 kg, BMI 24.2 +/- 2.9, VO2max 37.0 +/- 5.4) on a Velotron cycle ergometer: roughly 1.3 min to reach 85% HRmax in interval 1; time in the 85-95% band 2.7 +/- 0.6 min in interval 1 versus 3.4 to 3.5 min in intervals 2 to 4; 12.9 +/- 0.4 of 16 min overall; mean power 75%, 63%, 59% and 54% of peak power output across intervals 1 to 4. Three things that paper does NOT support and that I am therefore not claiming: its authors did not recommend setting resistance once, their method "continually adjusted [power] in steps of +/-5% PPO" off real-time heart rate and raised the work rate "at any point... that HR declined by >= 2 b/min"; the falling power was produced by that investigator control, not observed in self-paced riders; and the paper states its "data cannot be applied to older, inactive, or highly trained populations", which puts him outside it.

cues.name: Stay on the seat
cues.cue: Stay seated for all four efforts. Standing up is not a way to make an interval harder, and on a gym upright with flat pedals and street shoes it is not a skill you have yet. If the only way you can turn the pedals is to lift off the seat, the resistance is one level too high, full stop.
cues.test: Any moment during a 4 minute effort when your backside leaves the seat: sit back down and drop one resistance level immediately. No judgement about how briefly, and this override beats the 2:00 rule.
cues.why: All that paper supports is the narrow claim that standing does not change the metabolic cost of the work, in elite cyclists on a real bike. That standing is a bad idea for a 104.9 kg beginner on a gym upright is my judgement, not a finding: it costs him cadence control and it is the usual way "too much resistance" turns into a knee problem instead of into a dropped level.
cues.grounding: Carlsson M, Lindblom O, Carlsson T. Front Sports Act Living. 2024;6:1395415. Ten elite male cyclists (age 25 +/- 8, mass 75.9 +/- 8.4 kg), 5 min bouts at 6.8 degrees incline. Seated versus standing showed no significant difference in oxygen uptake (3.86 +/- 0.45 vs 3.86 +/- 0.42 L/min) or gross efficiency (21.3 +/- 1.2 vs 21.3 +/- 1.1 percent), identical to three significant figures. The study's actual primary comparison was a third condition, repeated seated/standing transitions (3.94 +/- 0.45 L/min, 21.0 +/- 1.1 percent), which is not what this cue is about.

cues.name: The four things that stop the effort
cues.cue: The run half of this plan has a hard stop, "any pain that changes how you walk means stop". The bike half is the only place in the week that goes near maximum, and it had none. Here it is. (1) KNEE: any sharp pain in or around the knee, or any ache that gets worse across an effort rather than staying level. Stop the effort, spin easy at the recovery resistance to the end of the session, and do not do the remaining efforts. (2) CHEST: pressure or pain in the chest, or pain spreading into the jaw, neck or left arm. Stop, get off, tell staff, and talk to a doctor before you finish or drive anywhere. (3) HEAD: dizziness, feeling faint, going cold and clammy, or your vision going patchy at the edges. Stop, get off, and sit down on the floor rather than on a machine. (4) HEART RATE ABOVE 175, higher than anything you have ever recorded: drop to the recovery resistance for two minutes, check the watch strap is snug first because a loose wrist sensor reads high, then decide whether the session continues. Everything else on this page is "drop one level and carry on". These four are not.
cues.test: Before each effort starts, one sentence to yourself: "chest, head, knee". Anything other than normal in any of the three, and the effort does not start. During an effort, if any of the four items above is present AT ALL, you stop rather than adjust. There is no severity judgement to make, presence is the whole test.
cues.why: I looked for a citable plain-language stop list for unsupervised interval training and did not find one I could read. What exists is ACSM's criteria for terminating a supervised exercise TEST, with a technician and an ECG in the room, and dressing that up as a source for a man alone on a gym bike would be exactly the kind of fake grounding this exercise is meant to catch. It is here because the alternative was no stop rule at all.
cues.grounding: CONVENTION

bike.cuesNote:
WHAT I DROPPED, AND WHY

1. SADDLE FORE AND AFT (the KOPS rule). Dropped entirely. It had no peer-reviewed support to begin with, and the test was broken in two ways at once: both branches described the identical geometry (spindle ahead of kneecap = kneecap behind spindle) while prescribing opposite corrections, and one of them was inverted. It also depends on where his head is rather than where his knee is, so leaning forward two inches flips the answer with the saddle untouched. It contradicted the saddle-height cue's own premise as well: if strangers move the seat post they move the seat rail. If his bike's seat slides, the honest one-liner is "leave it in the middle, write the notch number next to the height, put it back there each visit". That does not need a cue.

2. HANDLEBAR HEIGHT. Dropped. Three failures and no evidence: the Cureus bike-fit review isolates nothing about bar height, "set the bars level with the saddle" has no test he can perform while sitting on the saddle, and many gym uprights have fixed bars, so the prescribed fix ("raise them one notch") may not exist. The only part worth keeping is a sentence, not a cue: if you are propping your upper body up on your arms you are unloading the seat and quietly undoing the height you just set.

3. "INTERVAL 4 SHOULD BE ONE TO THREE LEVELS BELOW INTERVAL 1" AS A SUCCESS CRITERION. Dropped outright, and it was the worst item in the draft. Acala reports 75, 63, 59 and 54 percent of PEAK POWER OUTPUT. Gym resistance levels are an arbitrary manufacturer scale with no fixed watt value, so a 28 percent relative power drop cannot be converted into "one to three levels" from that paper or any other. Worse, as a pass/fail it manufactures a false failure: he could finish all four efforts in the heart rate band and be told the session did not succeed. The falling number survives only as reassurance inside the 2:00 cue, never as a target, and the success test is now heart rate alone.

4. THE CLAIM THAT ACALA'S AUTHORS "RECOMMEND PRESCRIBING BY POWER OUTPUT RATHER THAN CHASING HEART RATE MID-INTERVAL". Deleted. I fetched the paper and they did close to the opposite: power was "continually adjusted in steps of +/-5% PPO" to hold 85-95% HRmax, and "at any point during any interval that HR declined by >= 2 b/min, work rate was increased by 5% PPO". The 2:00 rule is now grounded on the measured lag (about 1.3 min to 85% HRmax) plus EX-MET's own "reached within two minutes", and the why says plainly that the single-decision design is my convention on top of a sourced fact.

5. THE PROPOSAL TO RE-READ HIS MAXIMUM HEART RATE OFF INTERVAL 4 IN WEEKS 3 AND 4 AND REVISE THE BAND UPWARD. Dropped. That turns interval 4 into a maximal test in an untrained 104.9 kg beginner, which is a different and higher-risk activity than the 4x4 he agreed to, and it ratchets every absolute target upward with no ceiling. His plan says 150 to 165. A cue sheet is not the place to renegotiate that upward. The honest caveat survives unchanged in cue 3: 175 is the highest figure his watch has recorded, not a measured peak, so the bands are probably slightly low, which is the safe direction.

6. "HIGHER CADENCE REDUCED KNEE LOAD AT EVERY POWER LEVEL". Deleted, because the source says the opposite in one place and it is the place that matters. Verified verbatim at the fetched URL: "The only exceptions were KAMpeak at 157 W and 210 W between 60 and 80 rpm". At the low power outputs a beginner rides, going from 60 to 80 rpm did NOT significantly reduce peak knee adduction moment, and that is precisely the comparison the prescription rested on. The whole knee-load argument is now a disclosed caveat and the cadence cue is labelled CONVENTION, justified by bookkeeping and by arithmetic (power = force x pedal speed) rather than by a study.

7. THREE CONTRADICTORY RULES FOR THE 1:00 MARK. The draft had cadence saying "check at 1:00, 2:00 and 3:00 and drop a level if RPM is below 75", the interval cue saying "no other checks during the four minutes", and a third cue adding a check at 1:00 of intervals 2 to 4. Worse, the cadence rule "RPM above 90 and heart rate under 150, add a level" fires almost automatically at 1:00 in interval 1, because the same document's own source says heart rate takes 1.3 minutes to arrive. There is now ONE checkpoint, 2:00, with a fixed priority order (cadence first, then heart rate) and exactly two standing overrides (off the seat, stop rule). The 85-to-90 RPM dead zone between the cue and its own test is gone.

MYTHS I AM CONFIDENT ENOUGH TO NAME

- "Get the saddle height slightly wrong and you will wreck your knees." Not supported. Bini & Priego-Quesada 2022, 41 studies: limited evidence on saddle-height changes and injury risk, and moderate evidence that changes under 4 percent of leg length produce trivial to small changes in lower-limb loads and no effect on oxygen uptake or efficiency. For a 90 cm leg that is roughly 3.5 cm of tolerance. Reproducing the same setting is worth more than measuring an angle, which is why the cue asks him to write a number down rather than hit 25 degrees.
- "Standing up makes the interval harder." It does not make the work cost more. Seated and standing were identical to three significant figures for oxygen uptake and gross efficiency in the study I read. It moves where the force comes from, that is all.
- "Your heart rate should be in the zone in the first minute." No. Measured lag was about 1.3 minutes in interval 1, and even with an investigator adjusting power every 15 seconds, only 2.7 of that interval's 4 minutes were spent in the band. Interval 1 is always the worst one for time in zone, by design of physiology and not by his failure.

WHAT I SEARCHED FOR AND COULD NOT GROUND

- Helgerud 2007, the original Norwegian 4x4. Not fetched, not cited anywhere. Everything asserted about the protocol comes from EX-MET and Acala, both of which I opened.
- A training RCT of the 4x4 on a bike in untrained or obese adults. I could not find one. What exists is the identical protocol on the identical machine in a clinical population (EX-MET, metabolic syndrome) and an acute heart-rate characterisation on a cycle ergometer in healthy ACTIVE young adults (Acala, mean BMI 24.2, mean age 26). The prescription for a 34-year-old BMI 33 beginner is a defensible extrapolation, not a tested one, and Acala says in its own limitations that its data "cannot be applied to older, inactive... populations".
- Peveler 2008 on saddle height and economy, the primary behind the widely repeated 25-35 degree figure. Paywalled at every mirror. Not cited. That is why no degree number appears in the cue text at all: both papers that restate 25-35 present it as background from previous research and neither tested it.
- Anything peer-reviewed isolating fore/aft saddle position or handlebar height. Nothing. Both cues dropped rather than dressed up with a bike-fitting blog.
- A citable stop-symptom list for unsupervised training. Not found. The ACSM material I located is for supervised, monitored exercise testing, which is a different setting, so the stop cue is labelled CONVENTION and says why.
- Cadence and knee load in anyone resembling him. Genuinely mixed: search surfaced findings in both directions (a 29 percent lower patellofemoral force at 90 vs 70 rpm in one study, no cadence effect on joint forces in another). I did not fetch those, so I have not cited them, and I did not build the cue on knee load.

TWO ASSUMPTIONS THAT COULD BREAK THIS SET

- I assume his gym bike has NUMBERED RESISTANCE LEVELS and a live RPM readout. Cue 4 gives the fallback if RPM is missing. If the bike has no numbered levels at all (a continuous knob), cues 4, 5 and 6 all need rewriting around a different unit, and he should say what machine it is.
- I assume the seat post carries numbers or countable holes. If it has neither, cue 1's whole point, reproducing the setting, needs a different anchor.

WHAT THE PLAN ITSELF STILL GETS WRONG

1. "10 min easy" and "3 min easy" carry no numbers, which is exactly the feeling-based instruction the house style bans. Cue 3 supplies 105-123 and 88-123, and note they are two different bands, not one.
2. Nothing tells him to record and restore the seat height on a machine strangers reset weekly. Cue 1 does.
3. No stop condition anywhere on the bike, although the run half has one. Cue 7 does.
4. 43 minutes is his structure, not the published one. EX-MET's session is 38 minutes because there is no recovery after interval 4. Harmless, but the 43 should not be presented as coming from the protocol.
5. HRpeak in the protocol means a peak from a maximal test. 175 is not that. Flagged in the cue he will actually read, not just in the notes.

OUT OF SCOPE: I did not check Wilson 2012, the interference-effect study behind putting the hard aerobic work on the bike instead of the treadmill. That rationale is his and unverified by me.

swim.title: Swim

baseline.label: Longest unbroken piece in the lap data
baseline.value: 600 m twice in one session, 11:36 and 12:11, on 2026-05-22. Then 500 m on 8 April, 22 April, 26 June and 14 August. Local dates, not the watch UTC dates.

baseline.label: What you said your limit was
baseline.value: 200 m without the buoy, on 2026-08-16. Both can be true if the buoy was in on the long ones, and on 2026-08-21 you did not remember which. Nothing in the export records a buoy, so the week-0 swim settles it.

baseline.label: What you actually do most swims
baseline.value: About 1,000 m in pieces of 50 to 150 m. Longest piece in your last ten swims: 100, 100, 100, 500, 125, 250, 150, 100, 150 m. The long one happens monthly, not weekly. That is the gap, not fitness.

baseline.label: Moving pace
baseline.value: 1:48 to 2:05 per 100 m on repeats. The 600s came in at 1:56 and 2:02, the 14 August 500 at 1:55. Pace is not what stops you.

baseline.label: Paddles ruled out
baseline.value: Stroke count on the 600s was 8.9 to 9.0 per length against 8.5 to 9.0 on your 50s and 100s. Paddles would drop that visibly, so those swims were unpaddled.

theGoal.whatThatActuallyIs: About 21 minutes, and 40 lengths of a 25 m pool. This file used to say your best continuous effort was "around 3 minutes". It is 11:36, and you did it twice in one session on 2026-05-22. The open question is whether the buoy was in, not whether you can swim for eleven minutes.
theGoal.whyItIsAchievable: You already cover the distance, at a decent pace, and have held more than half of it unbroken. The limiter is frequency: the long piece happens about monthly, so the skill never compounds.

theOneTechniqueChange.what: Swim the continuity piece 10 to 15 seconds per 100 m SLOWER than your normal 100 repeats. Around 2:05 to 2:10 per 100 m.
theOneTechniqueChange.why: This is the single thing that decides whether a long continuous swim works. Almost everyone who fails a distance swim fails it by starting at repeat pace. Going out slower is not cheating, it is the skill being trained.
theOneTechniqueChange.howToKnow: Set the pace off last session length times, per the calibration cue, and check length 1 afterwards. Do not judge pace by your breathing. If you need air, take it: dropping to every 2nd stroke is written into the plan, not a sign you went out fast.

swim.onDrills: Not prescribed, deliberately. Your strokes per length run 8.5 to 9.3 in a 25 m pool and your SWOLF is 35.6 to 39, which is a reasonable stroke, and the evidence that isolated drills improve adult freestyle endurance is thin. Pacing is the higher-value target. If you want drills later, they are a separate conversation with a real reason attached.

structure.note: Continuity piece FIRST, fresh and unassisted. After it the session is yours, around 1,000 to 1,200 m total. Every row below is measured from YOUR NUMBER, because how far you can swim unbroken is not yet known.

ladder.piece: Your number, then your number minus 100 m
ladder.note: Nothing new is being asked. This is the distance you just proved, twice, and the only change is that it happens EVERY swim instead of monthly.

ladder.piece: Your number plus 100 m, then your number minus 100 m
Your number plus 200 m, then your number minus 100 m
Your number plus 300 m, then your number minus 200 m
Your number plus 400 m, unbroken, then easy swimming with whatever is left
ladder.note: If your number was 600 m this row IS the goal. If it was 200 m this row is 600 m, which the data already shows you holding on a good day.

ladder.piece: Add 100 m a fortnight until the piece is 1,000 m
ladder.note: A fortnight, not a week. Never add distance after a fortnight where you missed swims: repeat the last one you completed.

calibration.name: Week 0: the swim that sets every number below
calibration.what: First thing in the session, one continuous piece. No buoy and no paddles, both left on the deck. Set the pace with the calibration length. Swim until the stop rule fires, stop at that wall, read the distance and round DOWN to the nearest 25 m. That is your number.
calibration.test: Was the buoy on the deck the whole time, and did you write the distance down before you left? If the buoy was between your legs the number does not count.
calibration.why: The data says 600 m, you said 200 m, and the buoy explains the gap but is not recorded. A fixed rung would be wrong by up to 400 m in either direction: written at 3 x 200 m it spends two months on a capacity you have, at 2 x 400 m it may not hold. One swim removes the guess.

paddleRule.rule: DORMANT: on 2026-08-21 you said you have not used paddles at all. Kept because it returns the day you pick them up: twice a week max, 200 m max, never in the continuity piece.
why: Withdrawn as a live constraint. The shoulder flag needed paddles and heavy pulling together, and
the paddles are not happening.
Schorn 2018, 193 amateur triathletes: paddle users had 24% overuse injuries against 10% for
non-users (p = 0.014), and paddles were an independent risk factor (p = 0.038) while swim
DURATION was not (p = 0.428). Heavier weekly weight training was a separate risk factor for acute
shoulder injury (p = 0.007), and that half still applies: pulldowns, rows and pressing four times
a week. Which is why the cap comes back on its own rather than being renegotiated.

swim.pullBuoyRule: Never in the continuity piece, so the number means something. The buoy is the only thing that explains 600 m in the data against the 200 m you reported, and nothing records it. Useful afterwards: a longer piece WITH the buoy teaches the pacing for a distance you cannot yet hold alone.

cues.name: The stop
cues.cue: You are allowed to stop, and a stop is not a failed swim. This rule outranks every other cue here. Three things end the swim, and you act on them in the water, not afterwards. (1) You take a breath you had not planned, twice, after you have already dropped to breathing every 2nd stroke. (2) You swallow water and cough. (3) You want to stop. That third one has no test attached and that is deliberate: wanting to stop is enough. When any of the three happens, finish to the nearest wall, stand up, and the swim is over at that distance. Write the distance down and go home. Swim in a lifeguarded lane, and swim in the lane closest to the wall or the lane rope so there is always something within one arm's reach. Do not use your watch's heart rate as a live guide in the water: wrist heart rate is unreliable when the sensor is wet and moving, so pace and breathing are the guide, not a number.
cues.test: Post-swim, one question with a yes or no answer: if you wanted to stop at any point, did you stop at the next wall? If you wanted to stop and kept swimming, this rule was broken, no matter how the swim ended. Separate post-swim check on the effort: the average heart rate the watch recorded for the continuous piece should be lower than the average heart rate it records for the 4 minute hard blocks on the gym bike. If it is higher, the swim was not easy, whatever the pace said.
cues.why: Nowhere in a swim is there a safe version of pushing through. Being short of air in water is not the same event as being short of air on a treadmill, and a 5x extension of his longest continuous swim is exactly where a novice runs out of options. A plan with no written stop turns every other cue into a reason to keep going.
cues.grounding: Instruction itself is CONVENTION. Context, fetched and verified: Toubekis AG, Beidaris N, Botonis PG, Koskolou M. Severe hypoxemia induced by prolonged expiration and reduced frequency breathing during submaximal swimming. J Sports Sci. 2017;35(11):1025-1033. Ten male swimmers (23.1 +/- 2.2 y, VO2max 47.3 +/- 7.2 ml/kg/min), 75 to 400 m at 90% critical speed. With prolonged expiration plus reduced-frequency breathing, 'oxygen saturation during recovery was decreased compared to starting values after 75, 100, 175, 275 and 375 m (78-91%, P < 0.05), while it remained unchanged after all trials in N condition (98 +/- 2%)'. Lactate 4.3 +/- 1.5 vs 3.3 +/- 1.7 mmol/L after 400 m. That is a harder breathing restriction at a harder pace than anything prescribed here, so it is not a prediction about his swim; it is the reason 'short of air' in water gets a written exit.

cues.name: Set the target from last week, then buy it with one length
cues.cue: Do not use a fixed pace number. Your target for the continuity swim is the middle length time from your last repeat session, plus 3 seconds. A length is one 25 m trip down the pool and the watch records a time for each one. If last session's lengths came in at 28 seconds, target 31. If they came in at 31, target 34. Your repeat pace spans 1:48 to 2:05 per 100 m, which is 27 to 31 seconds per length, so one printed number is wrong at one end of that range and the plan's '2:05 to 2:10' only fits the middle of it. Then buy the pace before the clock starts: push off, swim ONE length trying to hit the target, stop at the wall, look at the time on the watch. This is the only stop you are allowed, and it happens before the continuous swim begins. Came in fast by 2 seconds or more? Swim one more calibration length, aiming 2 seconds slower again. Then start the continuous swim.
cues.test: Post-swim, open the length list. Length 1 of the continuous swim must be within 1 second of your target and must not be faster than the target. Target 32 means length 1 reads 32, 33 or 34. Length 1 reading 30 means the swim started at repeat pace and the calibration did not transfer, whatever the rest of the swim looked like.
cues.why: The whole change in this block is 3 seconds per length. That is small enough that a first length which is only 'slightly quick' is not slightly quick, it is the old pace. And slow is the one thing he has never practised, so it will feel wrong and cannot be set by feel. The calibration length converts 'slower' into a number he has just watched appear on his own wrist thirty seconds ago. Arithmetic worth stating: 40 lengths at 31 to 33 seconds is 20:40 to 22:00, so this is a 21 minute swim.
cues.grounding: CONVENTION. There is no study behind this; it is arithmetic plus the watch's own definition of a length ('one trip down the pool'), which I read in the Garmin fenix swim terminology page.

cues.name: Every 3, and drop to every 2 on the next stroke, not at the next wall
cues.cue: Two words first. An ARM STROKE is one hand entering the water. An ARM CYCLE is both hands entering once, so one cycle equals two strokes. Start the swim breathing on every 3rd arm stroke, which makes the breathing side alternate: left hand in, right hand in, left hand in, breathe right; then three more, breathe left. The moment you notice you did not get enough air on a breath, take a breath on the very next stroke and stay on every 2nd stroke, same side each time, for the rest of the swim. Do not wait for the wall. That switch is written into the plan; it is not a failure and you do not revisit it mid-swim. Never go the other way: no every 4, no every 5, no seeing how far you can get without breathing.
cues.test: Count your own breaths on the length right after the halfway wall, and write the number down when you get out. On every 3rd stroke the number of breaths on a length equals your hand entries divided by 3, which at your stroke count is about 6. On every 2nd it is hand entries divided by 2, about 9. Intending every 3 and counting 7 or 8 means you were sneaking extra breaths in, which is every-3 already not holding: switch to every 2 for the rest of that swim.
cues.why: The symmetry case for alternating sides is real, and the endurance case for every 3 over every 2 is not, so the plan's 'keep it there' is over-firm and points at the exact failure the block exists to prevent. Given a snorkel and free breathing, swimmers took MORE than one breath per arm cycle at every intensity measured. Every 3 delivers 0.67 breaths per cycle and every 2 delivers 1.0, so every 2 is the closer match to what a swimming body spontaneously asks for.
cues.grounding: Both fetched and verified. Symmetry: Seifert L, Chehensse A, Tourny-Chollet C, Lemaitre F, Chollet D. Effect of breathing pattern on arm coordination symmetry in front crawl. J Strength Cond Res. 2008;22(5):1670-1676. DOI 10.1519/jsc.0b013e318182029d. Eleven expert male swimmers, seven randomised breathing patterns at 100 m race pace: 'breathing to the preferential side led to an asymmetry, in contrast to the other breathing patterns'; coordination was symmetric when breathing was bilateral, snorkel-axed, or removed.
